original_value: Text classification is an important and classical problem in natural language processing. There have been a number of studies that applied convolutional neural networks (convolution on regular grid, e.g., sequence) to classification. However, only a limited number of studies have explored the more flexible graph convolutional neural networks (convolution on non-grid, e.g., arbitrary graph) for the task. In this work, we propose to use graph convolutional networks for text classification. We build a single text graph for a corpus based on word co-occurrence and document word relations, then learn a Text Graph Convolutional Network (Text GCN) for the corpus. Our Text GCN is initialized with one-hot representation for word and document, it then jointly learns the embeddings for both words and documents, as supervised by the known class labels for documents. Our experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that a vanilla Text GCN without any external word embeddings or knowledge outperforms state-of-the-art methods for text classification. On the other hand, Text GCN also learns predictive word and document embeddings. In addition, experimental results show that the improvement of Text GCN over state-of-the-art comparison methods become more prominent as we lower the percentage of training data, suggesting the robustness of Text GCN to less training data in text classification.

result.paraphrase: Text classification is a long-standing and fundamental problem in natural language processing. While many studies have used convolutional neural networks operating on regular grids such as sequences for classification, relatively few have investigated the more flexible graph convolutional neural networks that work on non-grid structures like arbitrary graphs. Here, we propose applying graph convolutional networks to text classification. We construct a single text graph for a corpus using word co-occurrence and document-word relations, then train a Text Graph Convolutional Network (Text GCN) on the corpus. Starting from one-hot representations of words and documents, our Text GCN jointly learns embeddings for both under supervision from the known document class labels. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that a plain Text GCN, without external word embeddings or knowledge, outperforms state-of-the-art text classification methods. Text GCN also learns useful predictive word and document embeddings. Moreover, the gains over state-of-the-art comparison methods become more pronounced as the proportion of training data decreases, indicating that Text GCN is robust when training data is limited.
